opportunities.name: Month-end basis and index roll-off in the gas risk books

opportunities.name: Overriding MIPS zero volumes in POPS by hand
opportunities.summary: For outside-measured and mirrored (bidirectional) meters, measurement's system (MIPS) gets no volume until month-end, so its nightly file sends POPS a zero. That zero becomes the best available volume (BAV) and replaces the estimate Gas Control sends. POPS then passes the zero to Sitara, so purchase expense drops out of the desk's P&L and sits in the UA4 account. Pipeline Operations schedulers have to spot these zeros, get Gas Control's volumes and override POPS, then re-allocate the meter. A later nightly roll can write the zero back over a corrected meter, as happened at Valero Texoma on 3/21/2000. When a zero is missed, it takes an escalation by email: on 3/21/2000 Lauri Allen, Charlotte Hawkins, Michael Eiben and Gary Anderson wrote about it, and on 4/4/2000 Robert Lloyd had to ask again for Enron Methanol because his first note was not read as a request. The POPS team reported the bug to MIPS, but was told it was not a priority.
opportunities.change: Have the MIPS nightly file mark 'no data yet' as incomplete instead of zero, so POPS keeps Gas Control's estimate and schedulers stop overriding zeros by hand.
opportunities.explanation: Measurement would have its MIPS vendor (SPI) change the nightly file so that a zero sent because no data has arrived is tagged incomplete. Gary Anderson in measurement named this as the only possible fix; SPI was looking into it, and the cost was not yet known and might need a work order. POPS would then keep Gas Control's estimate as the best available volume until a real measured volume arrives. Schedulers would no longer search for zeroed meters, retype estimates, re-allocate, or redo the work after a nightly roll. The P&L and UA4 would no longer be wrong during the month, and the escalation emails would stop.

opportunities.summary: When a trading book grants origination to an originator group (for example FT-Central to IM-Central / Middle Market), the grant goes on the origination schedule and the receiving book records the origination on its own P&L as a separate step. Each evening an analyst in the P&L group (Gabriel Monroy, Binh Pham, Rahmaan Mwongozi) compares what each book recognized with the schedule. When they differ, the analyst emails the desk head (Darron Giron) with Michael Benien and Chris Abel copied. The desk head then has to find out where the amount came from, either by asking the analyst or by forwarding to a book administrator (Scott Palmer, Kam Keiser) or another lead (Kevin Radous). The analyst chases items that are still open the next night. The work stalls because neither side can see the other's entry: the receiving book records amounts that were never granted, or does not record ones that were, and someone has to search across books to find who granted what.

That one entry posts the origination to the receiving book's P&L, so the book administrators stop keying it a second time. The analysts' nightly comparison then only has to catch the rare manual adjustment, and if one does turn up it goes straight to the book administrator named on the grant. opportunities.name: Monthly set-up of HPL transport usage tickets
opportunities.summary: Before each month, someone rolls the Sitara transport usage tickets forward pipe by pipe. These are the deals Daren Farmer's desk uses to estimate transport cost in the P&L during the month. For June 2000, Heidi Withers worked through the HPL tickets on one day and the third-party tickets the next morning. She added the new month where it was missing, typed in the rates from the rate matrix and any baseload rates she knew of, and left volumes at zero on newly added months. Because of the zeroed volumes she asked the desk's schedulers to check volumes on all pipes in Position Manager. Third-party and newly agreed baseload rates are often not known when the tickets are set up, so the desk has to fix them later. The rates are typed in by hand, separately from the rates entered in Unify for invoicing, so they drift: in February 2000 a ticket had 0.055 where the matrix said 0.05, which throws off the in-month P&L. Tickets also get missed: in March 2001 the Midcon tickets at Oakville and Moore were not set up until a scheduler noticed. Sitara usage tickets cover only about three months each, so new tickets keep having to be made.
opportunities.change: Have Sitara roll each pipe's transport usage ticket into the next month automatically and fill its rate from the rate matrix, so staff key only the exceptions.
opportunities.explanation: Sitara would be changed so a transport usage ticket can run open-ended by pipe and path instead of about three months at a time. Before each month it would add the new month and carry the prior month's volume forward as the starting estimate, instead of zero. The ticket's rate would be read from the maintained transport rate matrix instead of typed in. The person who sets up the tickets today (Heidi Withers in 2000) would then only enter exceptions: newly agreed baseload or third-party rates, and new tickets such as a new demand charge. Schedulers would update volumes as they learn them, but would no longer need to check every pipe for zeroed months. A monthly list of pipes with flow but no ticket would catch any that are still missing.

opportunities.name: Seven Oaks meter 6884 monthly plant adjustment deals
opportunities.summary: Each month the plant operator at Seven Oaks (Teco, later PG&E and then El Paso) makes an adjustment at meter 986884. Depending on the month, this makes HPL a buyer or a seller. The arrangement was never written up as a contract, and the Sitara purchase and sale deals at the meter keep expiring or ending up under the wrong counterparty. When the allocation arrives with no deal to match it, Volume Management or Settlements cannot draft the volume. They park it on strangers gas and email logistics and the trader for deal numbers or extensions. This happened for May 2000, December 2000, and January, February, April and May 2001. In February 2001 the extension was blocked on the last day changes could be made, because Teco had been suspended as a counterparty.
opportunities.change: Set up standing (evergreen) purchase and sale deals with El Paso at meter 986884 so each month's adjustment can be drafted without asking anyone for a deal.
opportunities.explanation: Logistics and the trader (Daren Farmer) set up one evergreen purchase deal and one evergreen sale deal with El Paso, Teco's successor, at meter 986884. Both are priced the way the adjustment is settled today. Contracts, with George Weissman, would also write up the buy/sell arrangement, which runs for the remaining lease term, if they judge it safe to do so. In March 2000 Weissman was reluctant to raise it with Teco while other contracts were coming up for renewal, so the standing deals alone would still remove most of the chasing. Afterwards, Volume Management and Settlements allocate and draft each month's adjustment against the standing deal that matches its direction. They contact the trader only if a volume looks unusual or the counterparty changes again.

opp-01.audience: From the Portland real-time desk lead to BPA's contact for the generation services Enron provides (cc: the Frontier plant operator and Enron's services account lead)
opp-01.title: Request: automatic metering of Frontier (and GCPUD) hourly actuals to BPA, like the system planned for Grays Harbor
opp-01.body:
Subject: Request: set up automatic recording of Frontier's hourly actuals, as planned for Grays Harbor

Hello,

We're asking BPA to set up automatic recording of hourly actual generation for Frontier, and for GCPUD if it is still in the hourly check-out. This would be the same kind of system BPA said it would have in place for Grays Harbor by mid-August. With it, BPA would get Frontier's actuals every hour without a phone call from our desk.

Why: At the moment, a trader on our real-time desk calls Frontier every hour, around the clock, to get actual output. The trader then calls BPA to read the figure in, even for hours that were prescheduled. These calls happen while the trader is trading, and some hours have been missed. BPA has rightly raised this as inconsistent service. Automatic recording would make the hourly figures consistent, and it would end the problem rather than relying on better call discipline.

Could you reply with:
1. Whether the Grays Harbor approach can be extended to Frontier (and GCPUD).
2. What BPA needs from us and from the generator to set it up (meter or telemetry details, data format, a contact at the plant).
3. A likely start date.

We will keep making the hourly calls until the automatic feed is confirmed to be working.

Thank you,
Real-Time Desk Lead, Portland

---

Background (for internal readers and anyone who needs the detail)

How the check-out works today
- At the top of every hour, the trader on shift calls the generator (Frontier, and Grays Harbor until BPA's automatic system covers it) for its ACTUAL output, not an estimate.
- The trader calls BPA and reads in the actual figure. In June this hourly BPA check-out also covered GCPUD, with the call made between 25 and 35 minutes after the hour, right after the EPE dispatcher call.
- The trader initials the hour in the services book.
- The current instruction says this must be done even when the generator is prescheduled, and must continue "until these generators are automatically metered." So under the instruction already in force, automatic metering is the point where the calls stop.

Why this matters
- The calls compete with trading and have often been missed.
- BPA's contact said they were inclined to recommend to BPA that Enron is incapable of providing this service because of inconsistent performance.

What changes after metering
- Real-time traders stop the hourly generator call, the BPA call and the initialling.
- The desk steps in only if the meter feed fails. Before go-live we will agree with BPA how a failed feed is flagged, and the trader then goes back to the manual calls for those hours.

Estimated savings to the desk
- About 3 minutes per hour for Frontier alone. The instruction expects the whole process, when it covered two generators plus BPA, to take under 5 minutes.
- 24 times a day, which is about 730 a month, comes to about 36.5 trader-hours a month, or about $3,102.50 a month.
- Grays Harbor is not counted in the savings, because BPA was already automating it and it stops being a customer on Oct. 1.

Open points to confirm
- Whether GCPUD is still covered by the hourly check-out. If it is, include it in the request.
- Who at Frontier can provide meter or telemetry access.

opp-02.audience: Gas desk heads (all regions), with their book admins copied; sent by the Confirmations lead
opp-02.title: Request: a month-end MTM file by counterparty and region, so Confirmations can answer auditor requests without the desks
opp-02.body:
To: Gas desk heads (all regions)
Cc: Book admins who run mini-books for Confirmations requests
Subject: Month-end MTM by counterparty and region for auditor requests. Please reply by [date].

What we need:
From each month-end's official books, one file per region with three columns: counterparty short name, region and total MTM. No Delta/Vol. It should open in Excel and go to Confirmations every month-end.

Why:
Confirmations would then answer counterparty auditors' period-end valuation requests itself. Today these requests come in about 3 times a week, and each one goes to every desk. Your book admin runs a mini-book, blacks out Delta/Vol, exports it and emails it back, and then we combine the regional answers. That comes to about 75 minutes per request across all of us, or about 16 hours a month.

What we're asking each desk head to do by [date]:
1. Name the book admin on your desk who will produce your region's file.
2. Have that person produce a first file now for the year-end close (Dec 29 and Dec 31, 2000). Every auditor request we have seen so far is for those dates. Please tell us which of the two dates your official books use.
3. Agree that, from the next month-end, the file is produced from the official books on a schedule, ideally as an automated job, and saved where Confirmations can open it.

From then on:
- When a request is for a month-end or year-end date, Confirmations will look up the counterparty and reply to the auditor. It will not come to your desk.
- When a request is for any other date, it will still come to your desk the same way as now. That will continue until the on-line EnTelligence system, with back-dated curves, is built.

Thank you,
[Confirmations lead]

---
Background, for anyone who needs it

How it works today:
- A counterparty's auditor needs a third-party value of its trades with Enron, and the counterparty asks Confirmations for it.
- Confirmations has no system that values deals, so it emails the request to every gas desk head.
- Each desk head forwards it to a book admin. One example from the mail: "Call Pat Ryder for West desk requests."
- The book admin runs a mini-book for that counterparty as of the requested date, blacks out Delta/Vol, exports it to Excel and emails it back.
- Confirmations collects each region's answer and puts them together. The requests ask for this explicitly: "Please provide the total MTM value for that date within your region."

Recent examples:
- CoEnergy Trading Company, as of Dec 31, 2000
- CROSS TIMBERS, as of Dec 29, 2000
- "Two more counterparties need MTM values for Dec. 29, 2000."

What Confirmations has said about the cost:
"We do not have access to any system that values these deals, but are looking to get the on-line 'EnTelligence' built so that it carries back-dated curves that will allow us to complete these requests without taking up a Risk person's time and without having to black out information (Delta/Vol) that is included in a mini-book."

The month-end file takes care of most of this now, before EnTelligence exists. Risk staff no longer handle period-end requests. The file leaves out Delta/Vol from the start, so nothing has to be blacked out. Confirmations no longer has to collect pieces region by region.

Estimated saving:
About 75 minutes per request at about 3 requests a week (13 a month) is roughly 16 hours, or about $1,380, a month. The rate of 3 a week is what was stated. Only 3 requests appear in the mail from Feb–Mar 2001, so the actual saving may be lower.

opp-03.audience: From the gas risk lead to whoever maintains the gas risk calc (risk systems). Cc the gas book administrators and the regional risk leads.
opp-03.title: Request: make the prompt-month roll-off a scheduled setting in the gas risk calc
opp-03.body:
To: Risk systems lead (owner of the gas risk calc)
Cc: Gas book administrators; Regional risk leads
Subject: Request: make the prompt-month roll-off a scheduled setting in the gas risk calc

**My request:** Please add a roll-off calendar to the gas risk calc. On roll-off nights, one calc run should write two results:
- the 100% prompt-month basis to the TDS post ID
- the rolled-off basis to the Benchmark/V@R post ID

Please reply with whether this can be done and a date we could test it. If possible, test it before the next prompt-month roll-off.

**Why:** On each roll-off night, every administrator now calculates and officializes basis twice. They follow an email I send each month, and the sequence depends on people remembering it. In November, a missed reminder meant several traders' basis was not rolled off on the Benchmark, so V@R was wrong. The double calc also costs about 5.5 hours of administrator time a month (about $467.50).

---

**Details, for whoever builds or tests it**

What to build:
1. **Roll-off calendar setting, kept by the risk group.** It holds the roll-off dates and percentages for:
   - basis
   - Gas Daily and physical index (roll-off and roll-in)

   The current pattern runs over two nights: 50% of basis rolls off on the first night and 50% on the second. 50% of Gas Daily and physical index positions roll off and roll in each night.
2. **One calc, two post IDs.** On a roll-off night, a single calc writes the 100% prompt-month basis to the TDS post ID and the rolled-off basis to the Benchmark/V@R post ID. Administrators then calculate and officialize once, as on any other night.
3. **Exception check.** After the roll-off night's calc, a list of any book whose Benchmark basis was not rolled, sent to the gas risk lead and the relevant regional lead for follow-up.

What this removes:
- my monthly instruction email to the book administrators
- the second basis calc on each roll-off night
- the steps of unofficializing and officializing again between the two calcs
- relying on reminders between leads and administrators

Today's sequence, which each administrator repeats on both roll-off nights:
1. Calc the 100% basis calc.
2. Officialize.
3. Load positions into TDS.
4. Unofficialize.
5. Calc the 50% basis calc.
6. Officialize (this is the Benchmark used for V@R).

**Until the change is live:** Administrators should keep following the sequence above, and I will keep sending the monthly email. Regional leads: on each roll-off night, please confirm with every administrator in your region that the second calc was done. That step is the one missed in November.

**Savings basis:** about 330 minutes of administrator time per monthly roll-off. That is 5.5 hours a month, or about $467.50.

Thanks,
Gas risk lead

2. Tagg: Please save the calc we already use to find these deals as a query that runs every night. It should email Calgary settlements and the administrator of the book involved a list of any deal with ECC or a listed Canadian counterparty that is sitting outside FT-US/CAND-ERMS. That includes deals booked as ENA. The book administrator moves the deal the next morning.

Could you each reply by the end of this week with whether this can be done and a likely start date? We'd like it working before the next NYMEX close.

Thanks,
[Name], [Role]

---

Background, for anyone who needs it

How it works today
- Before each month's NYMEX invoicing, Calgary settlements searches the Houston books, makes a list of the ECC deals it finds there and emails 6 to 8 Houston staff. The email asks them to go through all their books and move ECC deals to FT-US/CAND-ERMS. That request is then forwarded to 5 to 7 book administrators, and each of them searches their own books.
- Invoicing for both ECC and ENA waits until this is finished: "Invoicing for November should start today, and both ECC and ENA are held back from invoicing until these deals are fixed."
- Most of the misplaced deals come from EnronOnline: "These are all EnronOnline deals so they were put into this book automatically." That's why a booking rule fixes the cause.

Why searching by hand still misses deals
- Only TransCanada Energy and Dynegy Canada are covered by the EOL rule today. Setting up the same rule for Duke was discussed with EOL but hasn't happened yet.
- Deals booked as ENA with a Canadian counterparty don't show up in Tagg as ECC deals, so they're missed by the search and need a second round of requests. In March: "I'm missing at least 10 deals from the April 2001 Nymex invoice." This is why the nightly query has to check the counterparty, not just whether a deal is marked ECC.
- A calc that finds these deals already exists, but people pass it around one at a time. Running it nightly for everyone replaces all the separate manual searches.

What changes
- No more month-end request asking everyone to search their books. Any deal that slips past the booking rule is caught within a day and fixed by the administrator of its book.
- NYMEX invoicing for ECC and ENA can start on time.
- Estimated saving: about 220 minutes per round, about 1.17 rounds a month (8 rounds between October 2000 and March 2001). That's roughly 4.3 hours, or about $365, a month, not counting the time saved by not delaying invoicing.

Before go-live
- Calgary settlements confirms the full list of ECC master-agreement counterparties.
- EOL confirms the rule covers every counterparty on the list.
- Tagg reporting confirms the nightly email goes to Calgary settlements and to the right administrator for each book.
- Book administrators confirm they'll move flagged deals the next morning.

opp-05.audience: Measurement manager (owner of MIPS and the SPI vendor relationship); cc POPS team lead, Pipeline Operations scheduling lead, desk accountant (UA4/P&L)
opp-05.title: Request: have SPI tag "no data yet" zeros in the MIPS nightly file as incomplete
opp-05.body:
To: Measurement Manager
Cc: POPS Team Lead; Pipeline Operations Scheduling Lead; Desk Accountant
Subject: Request: have SPI tag "no data yet" zeros in the MIPS nightly file as incomplete

What we're asking: Please have SPI change the MIPS nightly file so that a zero sent only because no volume has arrived yet is tagged (i) incomplete. Measurement already named this as the only possible fix. Please ask SPI for a cost and a date this week, and open a work order if one is needed.

Why: Right now these zeros replace Gas Control's estimate in POPS. That takes purchase expense out of the desk P&L and leaves it in UA4 until a scheduler finds the zero and overrides it by hand. This happens about once every working day, about 3.6 hours (around $307) of scheduler time a month. That doesn't count the P&L being wrong or the escalation emails.

Reply needed: whether you'll approve the change, and SPI's cost and date once you have them.

Thanks,
Pipeline Operations Scheduling Lead

---

Background, for anyone who needs it

How it works today
- MIPS gets no volume for outside-measured and bidirectional meters until month-end. Until then its nightly file sends POPS a zero ("systematically, no information equals zero").
- POPS takes that zero as the best available volume (BAV). It overwrites the estimate Gas Control sends, and POPS passes the zero to Sitara.
- If scheduling doesn't catch it, the desk's purchase expense is understated. The volumes "have not been picked up in [the desk's] P&L and are, instead, sitting in UA4."
- To fix it, schedulers find the zeroed meters, get Gas Control's volumes, override POPS and re-allocate the meter.
- A later nightly roll can put the zero back. On 3/21/2000 a meter that had been correct the night before was reset to zero from day 14 onward when the 14th rolled from MIPS, so it had to be fixed again.
- This affects "various bidirectional meters," not just one.

Where it stalls
- The POPS team reported the bug to MIPS and was told it was not a priority, so the hand work goes on.
- Missed zeros have to be escalated by email. Four people wrote about one on 3/21/2000. On 4/4/2000 an override request for Enron Methanol had to be sent twice because the first one, a sticky note, wasn't read as a request. The zero stayed in POPS for an extra day.

What changes after the fix
- POPS keeps Gas Control's estimate as the BAV until a real measured volume arrives.
- Schedulers no longer search for zeroed meters, retype estimates, re-allocate, or redo the work after a nightly roll.
- The desk P&L and UA4 stay correct during the month, and the escalation emails stop.

Savings estimate
- About 10 minutes each time, about once a working day (21.67 times a month) = 3.61 hours = $306.85 a month.
- This is a conservative figure. It doesn't include the time spent correcting the P&L or UA4, or the escalations.

Until the fix is live (Scheduling Lead and POPS team)
1. After each nightly MIPS roll, check the outside-measured and bidirectional meters in POPS for zero volumes.
2. Override any zeros with Gas Control's volumes and re-allocate the meter. Re-check meters you've already corrected, because a later roll can zero them again.
3. Send override requests by email with the meter, the days and "please override" in the subject line. Don't use sticky notes or verbal requests.

opp-06.audience: Manager of Financial Operations (from the Financial Operations coordinator who sends the monthly A and A Reclass notices)
opp-06.title: Proposal: post the monthly analyst charge automatically from the Org Database and notify only the charged managers
opp-06.body:
Subject: Change to the monthly A and A Reclass analyst charge – your approval needed

**What I'm asking:** Can we stop keying the monthly analyst charge by hand? Instead, I'd set it up as a recurring allocation (or scheduled upload) that takes the analyst count for each RC from the Org Database. Before it posts each month, it would send each manager whose RC is being charged the names of the analysts and the amount. Please reply with yes or no, and tell me who should build the allocation.

**Why:** We spend about 3.5 hours a month on this, which is roughly $297.50 a month. Right now we only catch errors after the entry has posted, so we end up doing correcting entries against a deadline. Sending the names before posting would catch those errors first.

**What would change**
1. Financial Operations sets up the analyst charge ($6,400 per analyst per RC) as a recurring allocation that reads the analyst assignments for each RC from the Org Database. We already use this source today.
2. A few days before it posts, each manager whose RC is being charged gets a short email listing the analysts' names and the amount. A draft is below.
3. If a manager sees a name that has left, they reply. We fix the Org Database before the allocation posts, so we don't need a correcting entry.
4. Managers who have no analysts get nothing and don't have to do anything. We stop asking all of the roughly 63 Energy Operations managers to look through their RC report every month.
5. Financial Operations reviews the allocation before it posts. We no longer build the headcount file or key the journal entry.

---

**Background (for anyone who needs it)**

How it works today:
- Corporate invoices Enron North America for all analyst program costs. Each month Financial Operations pulls a headcount file from the Org Database and makes a manual journal entry that charges $6,400 per analyst to each RC.
- We ask every manager on the distribution list to find the "A and A Reclass" lines on their RC report each month and check the count. In February's notice we wrote: "Please continue to check your RC report each month going forward."
- If the Org Database is out of date, for example because an analyst has left, the RC is charged wrongly. The manager then calls or emails us, and we process correcting journal entries before a deadline. In March's notice we wrote: "I have received a few calls and E-mails stating that some reclasses need to be made because you no longer have an analyst in your group." That round of corrections had to be done by Friday, March 3rd.

Why this should work:
- The charge already comes straight from the Org Database ("The information used by Financial Operations to charge your RC was obtained from the Org Database"). That means the hand-built file and the manual entry add work without adding any judgment, and an automatic allocation can do the same job.
- Sending names before posting moves the error check to before the charge is made. That is where it saves rework.

Savings estimate: about 210 minutes once a month, or 3.5 hours (≈ $297.50) a month. This covers building the file, keying the entry, and processing corrections.

---

**Draft pre-posting notice to charged managers**

Subject: Analyst charge to RC [RC number] for [month] – please check by [date]

Your RC will be charged for the analysts listed below this month, based on the Org Database:

- [Analyst name]
- [Analyst name]

Total charge: [count] × $6,400 = $[amount]

If anyone on this list is no longer in your group, or an analyst is missing, please reply to this email by [date] so we can update the Org Database before the charge posts. If the list is correct, you don't need to do anything.

Financial Operations

opp-07.audience: From the gas desks' origination schedule coordinator to the person who supports TAGG reporting and the desk spreadsheets, with the lead book administrators on each gas desk copied
opp-07.title: Request: fill origination schedule entries from TAGG by deal number
opp-07.body:
To: TAGG reporting / desk spreadsheet support
Cc: Lead book administrators, gas desks
Subject: Request: fill origination schedule entries from TAGG by deal number

Can you build two things for the gas desks' origination schedule?

1. A lookup keyed on deal number. When a book administrator types a deal number, it fills in Book, Date originated, Customer, B/S, Term, Price and Pub code from TAGG. It can be a spreadsheet macro or a TAGG extract, whichever is easier for you.
2. A daily extract of the Middle Market (NYMEX) group's TAGG deals. It adds any deal that isn't on the schedule yet, with $0 origination.

Why: Since January every entry needs 11 fields. Seven of them describe the deal and are already in TAGG, but admins type them in again by hand. Admins also have to type in every Middle Market deal just to record $0. We estimate the change saves about 8 minutes a working day, which is roughly 2.9 hours or $245 a month across the desks. It also cuts down on retyping errors in a schedule that feeds a daily report and is checked against each book's P&L every day.

Could you tell me by the end of the week whether this can be done, and which way (macro or extract) you'd go?

Lead book administrators: please reply with roughly how many entries your desk makes on a typical day. The estimate above assumes about five a day across all desks, and we have no actual count.

---------------------------------------------
Background and details (for whoever builds it)

How the schedule is filled in today
- Book administrators on each gas desk record every originated deal by hand in the origination schedule (the "origination file").
- From 9 January 2001, the Middle Market (NYMEX) group has received a daily report built from the schedule. That raised the fields per entry from seven to eleven:
  - Original fields: Book, Deal #, Date originated, Customer, Origination Group, Origination Value, Originator
  - Added fields, in this order: B/S, Term, Price, Pub code
- From 10 January 2001, every deal that group does must be on the schedule, including deals with no origination granted. Those get $0.
- Origination requests come in by deal number (for example, "The deal is HS Energy and the Deal number is V58190"). The admin then looks up the deal details and types them in.
- The schedule is kept up daily, and each book's P&L is checked against it every day. Past breaks include one desk recognizing origination that wasn't on the schedule, and another not recognizing part of an amount it had been granted.

What the admin would do after the change
1. Type the deal number. Book, Date originated, Customer, B/S, Term, Price and Pub code fill in from TAGG.
2. Type Origination Value, Origination Group and Originator.
3. Check the filled fields against the deal.
4. For Middle Market deals added by the daily extract, change the $0 to the granted amount on any row where origination is granted.

Where each field comes from
- From TAGG via the lookup: Book, Date originated, Customer, B/S, Term, Price, Pub code
- Typed by the admin: Deal #, Origination Value, Origination Group, Originator
- Added by the daily extract (Middle Market group only): any group deal not already on the schedule, with Origination Value set to $0

Requirements
- Keep the current column order, so the daily report built from the schedule doesn't change.
- Don't add an extract row for a deal that's already on the schedule.
- Let admins overwrite filled values if TAGG and the deal confirmation disagree.

Open questions
- How many entries are made per day on each desk? (Lead book administrators, see above.)
- Does the Middle Market (NYMEX) group's daily report need to change in any way once the $0 rows come from the extract instead of being typed in?

How the savings were estimated
8 minutes saved per working day × 21.67 working days a month = 2.89 hours, or $245.65 a month. This uses the stated rate of one round of entries per working day and an assumed volume of about five entries a day. The desk counts requested above will confirm or correct it.

opp-08.audience: Real Time Trading Support (from the Portland Real Time desk manager; cc the Real Time night shift traders)
opp-08.title: Request: automate the nightly El Paso model vs. CARP reconciliation entry
opp-08.body:
To: Real Time Trading Support
Cc: Real Time night shift traders
Subject: Request: nightly job to log the EPE reconciliation automatically

Could you set up a job or macro that runs each night after CARP finishes? It would:
1. Compare the day's El Paso model totals with the CARP report.
2. Write the totals, the result ("no variance" or "variance") and a timestamp into that month's EPE reconciliation file.
3. Email the shift only when there's a variance, listing the hours and deals that differ.

Why: Every night the shift fills in the reconciliation sheet by hand, even when there's nothing to report. Houston reads an empty sheet as a sign that nobody ran CARP. In the first 8 days of July there were no variances at all, but the entry still had to be made each night, and on at least one busy night it was missed. A timestamp written by the job would show Houston that CARP was run, and the traders would only have to explain real variances.

Could you reply with whether this can be done and a rough date? Until the job is running and checked, the shift keeps making the entry by hand as it does now.

Thanks,
Real Time Desk Manager, Portland

---
Background and details (for whoever builds it)

How it works today
- Since July 2001, at the end of each trading day the Real Time shift has to tie out the El Paso model with the CARP report. They log the El Paso totals in the reconciliation spreadsheet on the shared drive and explain any variances.
- The file is kept per month, for example: m://electric/epe/epe01/aug01/epe reconciliation model (with folders like July01, aug01).
- The sheet has to have an entry every night, even when nothing differs. That entry is only there to show that CARP was run.
- The reconciliation itself works well. The July checkout with Settlements took about five minutes, against the five days spent the month before. This request doesn't change the month-end process. It only takes over the nightly manual entry.

What the job should do
- Run after CARP has finished for the trading day.
- Read the day's El Paso model totals and the CARP report, then compare them.
- Write the El Paso totals, the result and a run timestamp into the current month's reconciliation file.
- At month change, create the next month's folder and file following the existing naming pattern.
- If there's a variance, email the shift the hours and deals that differ, leaving a space in the sheet for the trader's explanation.
- If there's no variance, nobody needs to open the sheet.

Questions for Real Time Trading Support
- When does CARP reliably finish each night, so the job can run after it?
- Where are the El Paso model totals and the CARP report read from, and are they in a format a macro can read directly?
- What should happen if the job fails or CARP hasn't run? A suggestion: email the shift so the entry is made by hand and the sheet is never left blank.

Suggested rollout
- For the first couple of weeks, run the job alongside the manual entry and check that the two match.
- After that, the shift stops making the manual entry on no-variance nights and only explains the variances the job flags.

Expected benefit
- About 5 minutes a night, every day: roughly 2.5 hours a month, or about $216 a month. It also removes the risk of a blank sheet caused by a forgotten entry, and the follow-up reminders that come with it.

opp-09.audience: From the RAR manager to the IT application owners for ERMS and RisktRAC and to the TAGG administrator, cc the desk risk managers
opp-09.title: Request: set up new ERMS curves in RisktRAC and TAGG automatically, with a nightly gap report
opp-09.body:
To: ERMS application owner; RisktRAC application owner; TAGG administrator
Cc: Desk risk managers

Subject: Request: set up new ERMS curves in RisktRAC and TAGG automatically, with a nightly gap report

What we're asking: Please help us replace the paper curve set-up form, the TAGG request emails and RAR's weekly manual check with one automated job. ERMS would be the master list of curves. When a curve is created in ERMS, the job would create the matching curve in RisktRAC and in TAGG, or queue it for RAR or the TAGG administrator to approve with one click. Each night the job would report any ERMS curve still missing from RisktRAC or TAGG.

Why: Right now a skipped step leaves positions out of V@R. In our first weekly check we "noted numerous curves in ERMS" that were not in RisktRAC. As things stand, "If the curve is not set up in RisktRAC the positions are not captured in the" V@R. The change also frees about 2.4 staff hours a month (about $200 a month).

Next step: Please reply with the person on each system who can say whether a nightly read of new ERMS curves is possible, and whether that read could either load RisktRAC and TAGG directly or feed an approval queue. Once we have those names, we'll set up a short working session to agree on the scope.

---

Background, for whoever needs it

How it works today
1. A desk risk manager builds a new curve in ERMS.
2. To get it into RisktRAC, the risk manager fills in a paper curve set-up request form and sends it to Risk Analysis and Reporting (RAR). RAR then keys the curve into RisktRAC by hand.
3. Separately, the risk manager emails the TAGG administrator to add the curve to TAGG and waits for a reply. Recent examples: "I have added two curves in Publ Names: WY/WELLHEAD and WY/MKTZONE. They are in curveview. Please add them to Tagg." and "I set up these new curves this morning and need them added to Tagg". The reply was "Done."
4. Because steps get skipped, RAR now compares ERMS with RisktRAC by hand every week: "Risk Analysis and Reporting has implemented a new process in which on a weekly basis new curves set up in ERMS are reviewed to ensure that these have been set up in RisktRAC."

What changes
- Risk managers create the curve once in ERMS and send no form and no email.
- The curve is created automatically in RisktRAC and TAGG, or it waits in a queue for one-click approval by RAR (RisktRAC) or the TAGG administrator (TAGG).
- A nightly exception report lists every ERMS curve not yet in RisktRAC or TAGG. RAR and the TAGG administrator only work the items on that report.
- RAR stops the weekly manual comparison.

Points to settle in the working session
- Should new curves load directly, or go to the approval queue first? Is the answer different for RisktRAC and TAGG?
- Which ERMS fields RisktRAC and TAGG need for each curve (the fields the paper form captures today).
- Who receives the nightly exception report, and who clears each item on it.
- Until the job is live, keep the current form and email steps and RAR's weekly check, so no curves are missed in the meantime.

How we estimated the savings
- About 33 minutes each time across the form, re-keying, the TAGG email round trip and the check. The weekly frequency stated by RAR is 4.33 times a month, which comes to about 2.38 hours, or $202.30, a month.
- The mail itself shows this work three times between October and December 2000. We used the stated weekly rate because it is the higher of the two.
- The larger benefit is risk control: positions no longer drop out of V@R because a curve was never set up.

opp-10.title: Starting next month-end: one P&L package per month for Arthur Andersen instead of per-book requests

To: Gas desk controllers

Subject: Starting next month-end: one P&L package per month for Arthur Andersen instead of per-book requests

What I'm asking for:
After each month-end close, a scheduled job will copy the P&L top pages and curve-shift reports we already produce for every gas book into one package for AA. We would stop forwarding AA's requests to the book administrators and stop gathering reports by hand. To set it up I need three things before the next close:

1. Each controller: fill in the book-owner list below for your books (the book and the administrator who owns it). Keep it current when ownership changes.
2. Whoever runs our month-end report jobs: confirm the job can find and copy, for every gas book, (a) the official P&L top page for the last business day of the month and (b) the top pages and curve-shift reports for the five days with the largest P&L, counted by size, gain or loss.
3. AA: tell us whether you can open a read-only folder on our side. If not, we will email the package to your Andersen addresses. You lost Lotus Notes access at the end of February.

Why: every month the same request goes from AA to us, from us to as many as seven administrators each, and then back. Items go missing and AA has to send second requests. If a controller is away, the request waits, because AA can't tell who owns which book. One standard package plus an owner list ends that cycle.

---

BOOK-OWNER LIST (to sit next to the package)

| Book / region | Controller | Book administrator | Date last confirmed |
|---|---|---|---|
| West Firm | | | |
| FT Northwest / North West Firm | | | |
| Mgmt. West | | | |
| Central Firm | | | |
| Central Intra-Month (IM-Central) | | | |
| Texas Intra-Month (IM-Texas) | | | |
| IM-East | | | |

---

Background, for anyone who wants it

How it works today:
- AA emails the controllers a list of books for the month. For each book they ask for the P&L top page for the last day of the month. Where curve shift drives the P&L, they also ask for "the P&L top pages for five of the largest days including the Curve Shift Reports."
- Each controller forwards the request to his book administrators, collects what they find and passes it to AA. Sometimes AA comes to pick up paper copies instead.
- Things slip. In October we got a second request for August that went from controller to controller to administrator before anyone pulled the reports. In December the West Firm, FT Northwest and Mgmt. West top pages and curve-shift reports were still missing from the third-quarter file, and they had to be pulled and copied by hand.
- In January one request covered IM-East, IM-Central and IM-Texas across two months and four controllers. AA was held up while I was away because, as they put it, "Is there someone else that can direct us to?" A week later they had to ask us to "direct me to the individual responsible for each of the desks listed below."

What changes:
- After close, the job puts (a) and (b) above for every gas book into one read-only package, or emails it to AA if they can't open the folder.
- AA chooses the books it wants to test straight from the package. They contact the administrator named on the owner list only to discuss what drove the P&L, which works the same as today.
- Controllers stop forwarding requests. Administrators stop pulling and copying reports. Second requests and "who is responsible" questions should stop.

What it saves: about 130 minutes of our time each month, roughly 2.2 hours or $184 a month. It also cuts the delays and the missing items, which this figure doesn't count.

What doesn't change: the reports themselves. The job only copies top pages and curve-shift reports we already produce. It doesn't create anything new.

If you see a gas book missing from the list above, or a reason the five-largest-days rule won't work for a book, reply to me before the next close.
